messages.author: 9450fe235592105e
messages.subject: R++
parts:
Hi all,

I was just noticing (for the fourth or fifth time) the lack of a "+="
operator in R and was wondering if any of you had a more intuitive
(and/or bugproof) method than the following

`+=` <- function(a='x',b) {e=parent.frame(); c=get(a, envir = e);
assign(a,c+b,envir=e,inherits=FALSE); c=get(a); c}

To use this, I have to type
`+=`('x',3)
to get the same result as, in other languages:
x += 3
or in R as
x = x+3
(or) x <-x+3

obviously, when a is something trivial like 'x', using the function at
top is a waste of hunting-and-pecking to find the tilde/accent and
apostrophe/quotes. However, my intent is to use it on matrix/array/list
elements.

I came across the following "need" for this function when I encountered
an element
aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1], ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k + 1]]
needed to change that k+1 to k+2 on left and right sides of an equation
where I was adding W
so it ended up as
aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1], ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k +
2]] = aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1],
ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k + 2]] + W
whereas
aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1], ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k +
2]] += W
or even
`+=`('aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1],
ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k + 2]]',W)

would be so much more compact and potentially (depending who you are)
more legible

Please tell me that there's a OverloadedCompoundOperators package
somewhere that accomplishes this more prettily and has ++ =+ -= =- --
etc already defined.

--Matt

messages.author: 8c8f0ca54c4a2459
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: R++
parts:
There's an incrementing function implemented in the `Hmisc` package. To increment by 1, you do:

    inc(x) <- 1

The `dec()` function does the same, but subtracts instead of adds.

Noam

messages.author: 244f5e4abbc229bf
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: R++
parts:
Erica,

The apply family of functions are not quite the same as true vectorization. The apply family of functions are mostly syntactic sugar for R loops. A vectorized function is one that actually pushes the loop to a low level implementation for performance/memory reasons. In general, the apply family of functions do not offer performance gains. Also, there is nothing wrong with using an R loop, which may be the best solution for a particular problem. In this case, Matthew likely needs to increment a variable in a loop and have control over that process and/or access to the variable. Most popular languages that have loops have increment/decrement operators. Unfortunately, R doesn't.


Jason

messages.author: 6e4e37c602c2b104
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: R++
parts:
Hi Jason and all,

When you use an apply function, the functions called within the “loop” are only looked up once, whereas in a for loop they’re looked up on each iteration. That typically provides significant time savings. For example:

> d = data.frame(x = rnorm(1e5), y = rnorm(1e5))
> system.time({
+   for(i in 1:nrow(d))
+       d$z[i] = d$x[i] * d$y[i]
+ })
   user  system elapsed 
 27.163  11.598  39.021 
> system.time({
+   d$z = sapply(1:nrow(d), function(i) d$x[i] * d$y[i])
+ })
   user  system elapsed 
  1.612   0.019   1.642

Sometimes for loops are necessary, but generally only when there’s interdependence among iterations. Maybe in some domains that’s often the case, but I suspect it is not accidental that R doesn’t have a built in increment function.

​Michael

+       invisible(d$x[i] * d$y[i])
+ })
   user  system elapsed 
  1.495   0.014   1.525 
> 
> system.time({
+   invisible(lapply(1:nrow(d), function(i) d$x[i] * d$y[i]))
+ })
   user  system elapsed 
  1.643   0.012   1.668
​



On Thu, Aug 13, 2015 at 11:07 PM, Michael Levy <mle...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Jason and all,

When you use an apply function, the functions called within the “loop” are only looked up once, whereas in a for loop they’re looked up on each iteration. That typically provides significant time savings. For example:

> d = data.frame(x = rnorm(1e5), y = rnorm(1e5))
> system.time({
+   for(i in 1:nrow(d))
+       d$z[i] = d$x[i] * d$y[i]
+ })
   user  system elapsed 
 27.163  11.598  39.021 
> system.time({
+   d$z = sapply(1:nrow(d), function(i) d$x[i] * d$y[i])
+ })
   user  system elapsed 
  1.612   0.019   1.642

Sometimes for loops are necessary, but generally only when there’s interdependence among iterations. Maybe in some domains that’s often the case, but I suspect it is not accidental that R doesn’t have a built in increment function.

​Michael

On Thu, Aug 13, 2015 at 10:30 PM, Jason Moore <moore...@gmail.com> wrote:
Erica,

The apply family of functions are not quite the same as true vectorization. The apply family of functions are mostly syntactic sugar for R loops. A vectorized function is one that actually pushes the loop to a low level implementation for performance/memory reasons. In general, the apply family of functions do not offer performance gains. Also, there is nothing wrong with using an R loop, which may be the best solution for a particular problem. In this case, Matthew likely needs to increment a variable in a loop and have control over that process and/or access to the variable. Most popular languages that have loops have increment/decrement operators. Unfortunately, R doesn't.


Jason

On Thu, Aug 13, 2015 at 10:37 AM, Erica Rettig <erica....@gmail.com> wrote:
I think the idea is that since you're not supposed to be extensively using loops anyway, the += has pretty limited utility. If you find yourself needing it a lot, you might think about  whether vectorized approaches like the apply family would be a better approach.

On Thu, Aug 13, 2015 at 7:02 AM, Noam Ross <noam...@gmail.com> wrote:
There's an incrementing function implemented in the `Hmisc` package. To increment by 1, you do:

    inc(x) <- 1

The `dec()` function does the same, but subtracts instead of adds.

Noam

On Thu, Aug 13, 2015 at 9:45 AM Matthew D. Pagel <pa...@cs.wisc.edu> wrote:

Hi all,

I was just noticing (for the fourth or fifth time) the lack of a "+="
operator in R and was wondering if any of you had a more intuitive
(and/or bugproof) method than the following

`+=` <- function(a='x',b) {e=parent.frame(); c=get(a, envir = e);
assign(a,c+b,envir=e,inherits=FALSE); c=get(a); c}

To use this, I have to type
`+=`('x',3)
to get the same result as, in other languages:
x += 3
or in R as
x = x+3
(or) x <-x+3

obviously, when a is something trivial like 'x', using the function at
top is a waste of hunting-and-pecking to find the tilde/accent and
apostrophe/quotes. However, my intent is to use it on matrix/array/list
elements.

I came across the following "need" for this function when I encountered
an element
aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1], ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k + 1]]
needed to change that k+1 to k+2 on left and right sides of an equation
where I was adding W
so it ended up as
aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1], ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k +
2]] = aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1],
ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k + 2]] + W
whereas
aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1], ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k +
2]] += W
or even
`+=`('aMatrix[ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r, 1],
ArrayOfVectors[[2]][[k]][r,k + 2]]',W)

would be so much more compact and potentially (depending who you are)
more legible

Please tell me that there's a OverloadedCompoundOperators package
somewhere that accomplishes this more prettily and has ++ =+ -= =- --
etc already defined.

--Matt

Hi guys...just an update. I wasn't able to figure out how to restructure the code that I was dealing with in an apply/vapply fashion, and it may be because the vectorized structure of the apply family takes away an order of information that I was looking to use. My memory of python's "map" function is that it keeps (tuple,s) together, which is something that I believe is close to a requirement for this to work with a map/mapply/vapply/apply.

Basically, I was using one two-column array/matrix as a lookup table to grab addresses from, then those addresses in a second n*n matrix would be augmented by a "fixed" but non-integer value.

In any case, sending the lookup table as the vector to act on wasn't working quite right, partly as it wanted to linearize the vector down the columns first. And putting the n*n matrix through the ringer was losing the information about which "cell" was being acted upon. I eventually got at the information I wanted to change (I think by rebuilding the linearized vector as.matrix again), but then the function was just spitting out the modified values, without actually modifying them in the base
table and not relaying the unmodified values as well as the modified values.

I was hoping to just use something like sum(NNMAtrixRow==LookupTable[,1] && NNMatrixCol==LookupTable[,2])*FixedValue as the inner function but I was getting no love.

Further, my little attempt to write a += function fails when you are attempting to update an element of a list/vector, which was kinda the whole point.

So, yesterday was not a good R coding day for me;)

I'll try some fiddling around again today briefly, but I guess I'm content with the loop structure for now, as it gets the job done. And it's ultimately not my code anyway :P

--Matt
